Show HN: Endo – A Higher-Order Harness
items.summary: Endo is a Higher-Order Harness (HOH). From the easiest concept to understand to the more complex ones, Endo gives you: * A single, simple UI to use any agent provider with your existing subscriptions, and hot-swap agents right in the middle of a session. * An orchestration layer, which I call HOH, allowing arbitrary composition of agents to achieve any workflow. A fun case I tried was asking Fable and Astra to mock a presidential debate. * An agent protocol that abstracts any agent. The key insight here is that every LLM is an agent—instead of treating the LLM as just one node inside an external ReAct loop. Endo was a concept formed while I was building OpenChart ( https://github.com/longsurf-ai/openchart ). To power trading workflows, I needed to support scenarios where strict determinism is required, while still keeping the flexibility of an agent's inference-time decision-making capability. A new form factor was needed between rigid n8n-style workflows and open-ended ReAct loop agents. Thus the creation of Endo. Endo is short for Endomorphism, a term rooted in category theory and functional programming. An endomorphism is a function that transforms an object into another object of the same type. Similarly, Endo itself is built purely on functional programming principles, relying heavily on Effect ( https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect ). ..And if you have patience to speak technical jargons, Endo is: * An agent orchestration layer—Higher-Order Harness (HOH)—where an entire agent is treated the same as a single LLM call, enabling arbitrary composition of extremely complex workflows. * A way to abstract any harness into a standardized protocol, where raw models and agents behave the exact same way, in a KV-cache-friendly manner. * A workflow engine that enables arbitrary composition of agents with a single workflow language. It's completely open source, and if you think this idea is cool, let's build together. Just for the fun of it.

A misbehaving test MCP server for stress-testing your MCP client
items.summary: We needed an MCP server that misbehaves on our command to test our own MCP gateway at work, but could only find well-behaved MCPs. That’s why we built a misbehaving MCP server ourselves and now share it on here, might be helpful for others building MCP gateways. It’s similar to the MCP Inspector, but lets you test your client not your server. We called it MCP Test Kitchen and it’s a (also hosted) MCP server that lets you: * Connect any client that takes a URL and an Authorization header (Cursor, Claude Desktop or your own). It answers both 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 clients and logs which protocol revision each request declared. * Pick one of 6 scenarios: HTTP transport errors, JSON-RPC error responses, tool results flagged isError, elicitation, multi round-trip requests (MRTR) via a C# SDK v2 scenario, and a baseline with a configurable delay. JSON-RPC and tool errors can be set to fail on a specific call, so the first call succeeds and the second fails. Resources and prompts are always on, each with a deliberately broken variant. If you want other scenarios, let us know. * Watch every request in a live log with timing, method, caller, status and protocol version. * Clone a TypeScript reference client, pinned to the latest spec, with full source. You can run it yourself, it’s open source. If you’d rather test it live, we also hosted it, but you need to login (Google or GitHub, needed for the token) and can get started immediately. We’d appreciate feedback, that’s why we're posting. In the live tool, there is a box that emails us directly. We’re around to check feedback + other scenarios you wish it had. * Link to the repo here: https://github.com/cakewalk-security/cakewalk-mcp-test-kitch... * Live tool access here: https://mcp-test-kitchen.cakewalk.security/login * More information on why we built this: https://www.cakewalk.security/mcp-test-kitchen/blog/wtf-simu...
